title: Inverted Full Pyramid
description: Brute force to optimized: per-cell space-or-star checks versus building the gap and shrinking odd-count star regions directly, then batching the whole pattern into one output call.

blocks.text: Given a positive integer n, print a centered pyramid of stars turned upside down, with n rows, where row i contains i minus 1 leading spaces followed by a shrinking, always odd, star count, so the widest row comes first and the shape narrows down to a single star at the base.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Pyramid Reflected in Water
blocks.text: Picture the same centered pyramid seen earlier, reflected upside down as if in a still pool of water below it. The widest layer is now on top, and every layer below it narrows by two stars while staying centered, the exact mirror image of the shape seen right side up.

blocks.caption: Row i is i minus 1 spaces followed by a shrinking odd star count

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The gap here grows as i minus 1, exactly the same growing gap formula already derived for the inverted left half pyramid, since both shapes are right aligned versions of a mirrored triangle.

Observation 2: The star count here shrinks, following 2 times n minus i plus 1, minus 1, which is exactly the full pyramid's odd formula, 2i minus 1, with i replaced by n minus i plus 1, the same substitution used to mirror the inverted right half pyramid from the plain one.

Observation 3: So nothing about this shape is genuinely new, it is the growing gap already known from one earlier problem, combined with the shrinking odd star count derived by mirroring another.

Observation 4: Since both region lengths are still fully known before each row is built, the same direct-construction and single-call output batching used throughout this division apply here without any further changes.
That reasoning turns what looks like the hardest shape in the division into a straightforward combination of two formulas already derived elsewhere.

Use an outer loop for each row i, and an inner loop that checks every column this row actually uses, deciding for each one individually whether it still falls inside the leading gap or has reached the star region.

items: Loop over each row i from 1 to n.
Compute the gap size, i minus 1, and the star count, 2 times n minus i plus 1, minus 1.
Check every column from 0 up to the row width minus 1.
If the column is still within the gap, print a space, otherwise print a star.
After finishing a row, move to the next line.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: check every column position and decide space or star

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: gap and stars are both computed once per row, before the inner loop begins, using formulas that combine the growing gap from one earlier problem with the shrinking odd star count from another.
The inner loop's bound, gap plus stars, is exactly the total width this row uses, so every column that matters gets checked exactly once, in order.

The comparison j less than gap decides space or star for a single column at a time, even though this same boundary never moves within the row, which is exactly the inefficiency the optimized version removes.

blocks.text: This is correct, since every column position in every row is individually checked and assigned the right character, keeping each row centered above the next as the shape narrows.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), since the total stars across all rows is 2n minus 1 down to 1, proportional to n squared, and every position is checked individually.
Space: O(1) extra space, no string is ever built.

Limitation: checking every column position one at a time wastes a per cell decision that never changes within a row, since both the gap size and the star count for row i are already known before the row even starts. Both regions can instead be built directly in one operation each, with no per cell checking at all.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why checking every column works but is wasteful: the same gap-versus-star boundary, fixed at column i minus 1 for the entire row, gets re-checked on every one of that row's columns instead of being used once.

What stays the same as every other pattern in this division: the underlying insight, both region lengths are known before the row starts, so both can be built directly.

What is different here: both formulas are themselves combinations of earlier ones, a growing gap borrowed from the inverted left half pyramid and a shrinking odd star count derived by mirroring the full pyramid.

Can the same direct-construction technique be reused unchanged: yes, a repeat operation still builds each region in one step regardless of how its formula was derived.

The core idea: build the growing gap directly at length i minus 1, build the shrinking odd star region directly at its computed length, concatenate them, then print the row once.

For each row i, build the leading gap and the star region directly, using one operation for the i minus 1 spaces and another for the shrinking star count, then concatenate them into a single row string. This removes all per cell branching, needing only one print call per row.
For each row i, build the growing gap and the shrinking odd star region directly, one operation each, then concatenate them into a single row string and print it once.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: build the spaces and shrinking star count directly, one print call per row

codes.python:
def inverted_full_pyramid(n):
    for i in range(1, n + 1):                  # row i needs i - 1 spaces then a shrinking star count
        stars = 2 * (n - i + 1) - 1
        row = " " * (i - 1) + "*" * stars          # build spaces and stars directly, no per cell checks
        print(row)                                # one print call per row instead of per character


if __name__ == "__main__":
    inverted_full_pyramid(4)

blocks.text: This works because both of row i's region lengths, i minus 1 for the gap and 2 times n minus i plus 1, minus 1, for the stars, are fully known ahead of time, each one derived by combining formulas already established elsewhere in this division; a direct repeat operation still constructs each region in one step, with no dependence on any other row. As i increases from 1 to n, the gap i minus 1 grows from 0 up to n minus 1, while the odd star count shrinks from 2n minus 1 down to 1, and concatenating the two produces exactly the right, narrowing, centered row every time.

items: The star count is computed as 2 times n minus i plus 1, minus 1, and the gap as i minus 1, directly inside the outer loop, each formula a direct combination of ones already derived for earlier problems in this division.

Two direct repeat operations construct the gap and the shrinking odd star region separately, exactly the same construction technique used everywhere else in this division, then concatenation joins them into the finished row.

Each row is printed immediately after being built, one output call per row, with both the growing gap and the shrinking odd star count handled entirely by their formulas, not by any special casing in the loop itself.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared) total characters produced, the same as the brute force, but with no per cell branching and only O(n) print calls instead of O(n squared) checks.
Space: O(n), for the single row string being built and printed at a time.
10. Further Optimization: A Single Output Call

Every row is already being built directly in one operation, so instead of printing each one separately, all n rows can be built first, joined together with newline characters, and the entire pattern can be produced with a single output call.

blocks.caption: Further optimization: join every row into one string and output it in a single call

items: Every row is still built directly from its own growing gap, i minus 1, and shrinking odd star count, exactly as in the optimized version, the only change is deferring output until every row exists.
Joining all n rows with newline characters assembles the complete inverted, centered pattern as a single string, entirely in memory, before any output call happens.
A single print call at the very end outputs the whole pyramid, cutting the operation count down to exactly 1 regardless of how large n is.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), the same total characters produced.
Space: O(n squared), to hold every row joined into one string before the single output call. This trades some memory for the fewest possible output calls, exactly one, no matter how large n is.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "how is this related to the full pyramid", think: substitute n minus i plus 1 for i in the odd star count formula, and flip the gap from shrinking to growing.
If the interviewer says "can you avoid checking every column", think: build the growing gap and the shrinking odd star region directly, using their known lengths.
If the interviewer says "can you reduce this to one output call", think: build every row first, join with newlines, print once.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: All three versions produce the same O(n squared) total characters, since that is fixed by the shape itself. What changes is how that output is organized: per cell checks in the brute force version, one formula built row per print call in the optimized version, and exactly one call for the entire pattern in the further optimized version.

items: Pattern: pattern printing that mirrors the full pyramid both top to bottom and formula by formula, a growing gap combined with a shrinking, always odd, star region.

Core Idea: row i always needs exactly i minus 1 spaces and a shrinking odd star count, 2 times n minus i plus 1, minus 1, both lengths derived by combining formulas already known from earlier problems in this division, so two direct repeat operations construct each region in one step.
Time: O(n squared) checks for the brute force, O(n) output calls for the optimized version, O(1) for the further optimized version; total characters printed are always O(n squared).
Space: O(1) extra for the brute force, O(n) for the current row, O(n squared) for the fully joined pattern.
Most Important Observation: a shape that looks entirely new can often be assembled from formulas already derived for two separate, earlier problems.
Interview Difficulty: easy to produce the correct shape by trial and error; explaining exactly which two earlier formulas were combined, and how, is what shows real pattern recognition.
One line memory trick: growing gap i minus 1 from the inverted left half pyramid, shrinking odd stars from mirroring the full pyramid, build both directly and concatenate.
